Chapter 1: Building a Name and Hiding the Source
You know that feeling when you walk through a museum or a hospital wing and spot a family’s name engraved in marble?
There’s a certain comfort in it—almost like a quiet promise that someone cared enough to give back, to make things better for everyone.
For decades, the Sackler name was everywhere—university buildings, art galleries, medical research centers. It became part of the background, woven right into the fabric of culture and progress.
Most folks never really stopped to wonder where all that money came from. It just seemed to appear, like magic, with no strings attached.
But behind those polished plaques and generous gifts was a story almost nobody knew.
The Sackler family—whose fortune seemed to materialize out of thin air—had built their wealth in ways that were hidden from public view.
Their journey started back in the early twentieth century, shaped by tough times, big ambition, and a relentless drive to break out of their circumstances.
Picture this: three brothers—Arthur, Mortimer, and Raymond—growing up in Brooklyn as the sons of Jewish immigrants. Their parents worked hard, but the family never had much.
The world wasn’t always welcoming, either. Anti-Semitism was part of everyday life, and doors to opportunity weren’t exactly wide open.
But these brothers were determined to make something of themselves. Medicine became their way forward—not just a job, but a path to respect and security.
Arthur, the oldest, was the visionary. He had this knack for spotting possibilities where other people just saw roadblocks.
While he worked as a psychiatrist, Arthur became fascinated with advertising. He realized something important: the way a drug was marketed could be just as powerful as the drug itself.
That insight wasn’t just clever—it would end up shaping the Sackler legacy in ways nobody could have imagined.
After World War II, Arthur started to blur the line between medicine and marketing. He didn’t just treat patients—he sold big ideas.
He convinced doctors that new medicines could change lives, and he used every tool he had—magazines, medical conferences, even ghostwritten articles—to get his message out.
The pharmaceutical industry was transforming, and Arthur was right there at the front of the wave.
Meanwhile, Mortimer and Raymond followed his lead. They set up their own medical practices and invested in a small, struggling pharmaceutical company called Purdue Frederick.
At first, Purdue was nothing glamorous—just a business selling earwax remover and laxatives. But the Sacklers saw something others didn’t.
They believed that, with the right approach, they could turn it into something much, much bigger.
Over the years, the family’s fortune grew. And so did their desire for privacy.
They were generous with donations, but always careful to keep the source of their money hidden away.
The Sacklers wanted to be seen as benefactors, not businessmen. And for decades, that’s exactly how the world saw them—connected to culture, education, and healing, not to commerce or controversy.
Most people just accepted the story at face value. They saw the family’s philanthropy and assumed it came from pure generosity.
But underneath it all, the Sacklers were quietly building an empire—one that would eventually change American medicine and public health forever.
It’s easy to admire a name carved into stone. But it takes a little more courage to ask where the money really came from, or what it might have cost.
The Sacklers knew this better than anyone. They were masters at shaping their reputation, using philanthropy as a shield.
For a long time, it worked.
But the truth—well, the truth always finds a way out.
